#795. DWTS’ Sharna Burgess Slams Fans for Using Voting to "Manipulate" Show

Dancing With the Stars pro Sharna Burgess accused fans of using the voting system to “vote people off” and “manipulate the show” following Harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Johnson’s Nov. 17 elimination.

Sharna Burgess believes Dancing With the Stars fans took a wrong turn with the latest elimination.

Days after frontrunners Harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Johnson were sent home during the show's semifinals Nov. 17, the DWTS pro detailed her theory behind their exit, accusing viewers of using the voting system to eliminate contestants they don’t like rather than supporting their favorites.

“Sadly no, I felt it was going to be another shock elimination,” Burgess wrote on her Instagram Stories Nov. 20, replying to a fan who asked if she was surprised Shum and Johnson were sent home. “Not because they deserved it but simply because the online discourse is so wild that [it] was pretty clear who fans were ‘voting off’ and how they have felt about dance experience contestants.”

But according to the 41-year-old—who was paired with Bachelor Nation’s Tyler Cameron for season 35 before their Oct. 27 elimination—the issue is much bigger than a single misstep.

“[It’s] so disappointing to see our voting system is now being used by viewers to vote people off instead of voting for your favorite,” Burgess continued, before pointing to how fans can cast 20 votes per couple. “I say we got [sic] back to yall only have 10 votes total and you have to figure out how to dish them out.”

As the professional dancer put it, “This voting ppl off thing is so insanely negative and not what we are built on and it's seemingly given fans the chance to manipulate the show. JMO.”

On the Nov. 17 episode, Shum, 44, and Johnson, 32, were eliminated despite receiving perfect scores on both of their dances. This marked the second week in a row a frontrunner pair—which also featured a celebrity with previous dance experience—was sent home, as Johnson’s husband Val Chmerkovskiy and his partner Jenna Dewan were voted off the week prior.

As for the Grey’s Anatomy star’s thoughts on his elimination?

“I oddly feel at ease. I don't feel sad—it's really weird,” Shum told E! News in an interview after his elimination. “I kind of felt like we accomplished everything we wanted to.”

As Dancing With the Stars spins into the season 35 finale, keep reading for a closer look at the show’s secrets…

How Much Do the Celebrities Get Paid to Be on Dancing With the Stars?

Citing multiple sources, Variety reported in 2019 that Dancing With the Stars contestants make $125,000 for the rehearsal period and first two weeks of the show. If they progress beyond that point, the outlet continued, they earn more money each week. At the time, sources told the publication stars could earn a maximum of $295,000.

However, Bobby Bones said he made more than this when he won season 27 with Sharna Burgess in 2018.

"That show pays OK," the radio personality said on a Sept. 2025 episode of Jason Tartick's podcast Trading Secrets. "Like, first episode, no money. Second episode, $10,000. I think it's like, $10,000, $10,000, $20,000, $20,000. It ends up being $50,000 an episode if you last."

Also receiving a base salary of around $110,000, Bones continued, "I ended up making close to $400,000 from that show."

ABC has not publicly confirmed any of these figures.

What Do the Pros Get Paid on Dancing With the Stars?

Similarly, little has been shared publicly about how much the pros get paid. But as with the contestants, it seems like the longer they're on the show, the more money they can make.

But even if a pro is eliminated in the first round, they're not leaving the ballroom empty-handed.

"You're guaranteed until a certain amount of weeks," Jenna Johnson said on a June 2025 episode of Kelly Stafford and Hank Winchester's podcast The Morning After. "I think there's different contracts though. I can't speak for everybody."

Do Pros Get Paid More If They Win Dancing With the Stars?

While Johnson—who won season 26 with Olympic figure skater Adam Rippon, as well as season 33 with The Bachelor's Joey Graziadei—says the pros don't get a larger paycheck if they take home what is now called the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy, she noted there's still an incentive to make it to the finale (besides bragging rights, of course).

"If you make it all the way to the end, you're getting paid the whole season, which is amazing, and you get a bonus on top of that for making it to the finale," she explained on The Morning After. "If you win, it's not like you win a $1 million and split it with your partner. You're just getting a cute trophy together."

Do the Troupe Members Get Paid as Much as the Pros on Dancing With the Stars?

On a 2022 episode of Trading Secrets, Lindsay Arnold recalled how her salary was cut "more than in half" when she was demoted from pro to troupe member.

How Are Pros and Celebrities Paired Together on Dancing With the Stars?

The pros get little input when it comes to being matched with a celebrity.

"You get no say," Lindsay said on a May 2025 episode of Maggie Sellers' Hot Smart Rich podcast. "It's very much just, 'Here's your partner. Make it work.'"

In fact, Jenna said the pairing is often a secret until the last minute.

"They really want to keep it a secret until you meet them live," Jenna said on The Morning After. "They want that genuine reaction. So I think people always think we know who we have and we're keeping it a secret. Absolutely not. They do not tell us. They really don't even want us to know the cast. It gets leaked a lot, but they want it very hush-hush until you walk in and meet your partner."

As for what the Dancing With the Stars team looks for when making these matches?

"It's based on height, build and personality and compatibility," former showrunner Rob Wade told E! News in 2015. "We don't pair people who aren't going to get on. It's too intense. It's not like The Bachelor or something, we couldn't do that. That would just be miserable experience for the celebrity, for us and the viewer. You don't want to see two people who don't like each other and, quite frankly, we have made that mistake pairing people up who didn't get on so well."

How Often Do the Pros and Celebrities Practice on Dancing With the Stars?

Put simply, a lot."Every day we have four-hour rehearsals," Rylee Arnold, who was partnered with Olympic gymnast Stephen Nedoroscik on season 33, shared on a September 2024 episode of the Lightweights Podcast With Joe Vulpis. "It’s either 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m., 1:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. or 5:00 p.m to 9:00 p.m."But the work doesn't stop once the rehearsal wraps. Rylee noted she might then meet with producers or the creative team, work on choreography or study dance videos."Literally my whole life is devoted to it," she continued, "but it's my passion and it's what I love. So, it makes me so happy."Indeed, it's a no-days-off kind of gig."We have our show day on Tuesday and then it's Wednesday to Sunday, straight rehearsals," Rylee added. "And then Monday we have camera blocking and then Tuesday's show day again."

Do the Pros Get to Pick the Songs Each Week for Their Dance With Their Celebrity Partner?

"Mostly yes," Emma Slater and Britt Stewart revealed in a September 2025 Instagram video, "though it's a collaboration with producers."

What's the Process Like for Making the Costumes for Dancing With the Stars?

If you thought the quickstep was fast, just wait until you hear about the pace of the costume department."We meet with the set and lighting designers, dancers and talent and create a story [for each pair]," costume designer Daniela Gschwendtner told TV Insider back in 2017. "Then we sketch out ideas. We have five days, max, to make all the outfits. That’s half a day per costume, not including all the rhinestones. The fitting and trimming we do later. We have about 20 people in our department and then we have a separate tailor shop. It’s a big enterprise."In fact, costume designer Steven Norman Lee said pairs usually try on their costumes for the first time just hours before showtime. And while the department "might use a pair of pants again for the boys," he continued, everything is generally made custom each week.As Gschwendtner added, "We do reuse things for group numbers or promo shoots, but not for the competition. We don’t reuse things unless there’s a specific reason to do so. We try to keep everybody fresh and new in something different every week, so it stays interesting."

Thermal satellites from an Indian startup aim to spot urban heat, crop stress and wildfires from orbit.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

AHMEDABAD, India — As climate disasters grow more frequent and severe, a young Indian space-tech startup is betting it can help the world act sooner by reading Earth's temperature from orbit in near-real time.

SatLeo Labs, based here in western India, is building what it calls a "thermometer for Earth" in space. It plans to achieve its roadmap to deliver frequent, near-real-time thermal data through Pyro, a planned constellation of 15 microsatellites that will circle the planet in low Earth orbit by early 2030, if all goes to plan. Equipped with thermal sensors and onboard artificial intelligence, the satellites will measure the heat radiating from Earth's surface at a resolution finer than 10 meters (33 feet), which is sharp enough to map heat variations down to street level, the company says.

"It's going to be that precise," SatLeo Labs co-founder Urmil Bakhai told Space.com in a recent interview.

That level of detail, he said, helps distinguish temperatures across a single city and pinpoint urban hot spots, allowing governments and policymakers to plan targeted interventions and more heat-resilient city designs.

The company is also targeting agriculture, and for good reason: Research suggests that thermal data can directly reveal water stress on crops days before leaves wilt, discolor or show other visible damage, unlike visible-light satellite imagery. Other uses the company is eyeing include spotting forest fires early, tracking industrial emissions and, on the defense side, detecting sudden temperature spikes from missile launches.

Down the road, the team also envisions hyper-local uses. Near the top of its list are live heat maps built into navigation apps that could help gig-economy workers in India. These folks, who often ride motorcycles, could use the data to pick cooler routes during heat waves, said Bakhai.

"We are in space, but we're solving problems on Earth," said Shravan Bhati, SatLeo's co-founder and CEO.

First, however, the company has to prove that its homegrown hardware works in space. On Oct. 1, SatLeo launched its first technology demonstrator, TAPAS-1, aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket as part of the Transporter-18 rideshare mission. Short for "Thermal Access Platform for Analytics & Solutions," TAPAS-1 is India's first commercial thermal payload in orbit and the first of SatLeo's three planned test payloads meant to validate its technology.

Once complete, the 15-satellite Pyro fleet will scan all of the world's land surface at least twice a day, Bakhai said. Successful deployment of that fleet would make SatLeo one of just a few private thermal-imaging operators across the world, such as SatVu in the U.K. and OroraTech in Germany.

The company has raised roughly $6 million since it was founded in 2023, and it holds letters of intent worth $54 million from prospective customers, Bakhai said.

SatLeo grew out of a government project that used satellite data for farming insights. Its founders found existing thermal data, such as from the U.S. government's Landsat satellites or Earth-observing craft operated by the San Francisco company Planet Labs, too coarse for India's fragmented farmlands, Bakhai said. When field teams and drones couldn't fill the gap at scale, "we realized space is the only solution," he said.

SatLeo's orbital ambitions take shape on the ground, inside a light-blocked cleanroom at the company's headquarters here in Ahmedabad. When Space.com visited in late October, about three weeks after TAPAS-1 launched, a handful of engineers in cleanroom coats were already fine-tuning its successor, TAPAS-2.

The payload itself sat perched on a solitary, nondescript table with a thick, hole-filled steel top meant to dampen vibrations from footsteps, traffic and the like. The room's only window was covered by a thick black blind to seal out stray light, a necessity for calibrating sensors meant to track the planet's thermal pulse from a few hundred kilometers up.

Despite its small size, the payload is built to collect enormous amounts of data. How much detail a payload can capture "all depends upon the architecture of the detector," said SatLeo co-founder Ranendu Ghosh, a former scientist at the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO).

The design captures two infrared bands, mid-wave and long-wave, on the same payload. The company says this lets a single design serve both civilian and defense uses: long-wave suits applications like agriculture, while the hotter signatures of fires or missile launches show up better in mid-wave.

TAPAS-1 took just six months to build, and TAPAS-2 is on a similar timeline: It's expected to be ready by February 2027, according to the team.

Access to government test facilities explains much of that speed, Bhati said. Rather than buy capital-intensive equipment, such as a thermal vacuum chamber that mimics conditions in space, the company calibrates its payloads at facilities run by IN-SPACe, the government agency that supports private space firms, and ISRO's Space Applications Centre, both in Ahmedabad.

A small group of former ISRO scientists, about eight among a staff of around 40, also mentored the younger workforce and "really made this journey a little faster for us," Bakhai said.

Ghosh, who spent more than two decades at ISRO, said the nature of a private company helps, too. "When I was in ISRO, I saw people delivering this kind of a payload," he said. "I never saw it delivered in less than a year."

He credited the SatLeo team's "zeal to deliver in time," along with fewer administrative challenges than at ISRO, which he described as an organization where "you cannot bypass the hierarchy."

The harder constraint, the founders said, is not building satellites but finding rockets to carry them to space. TAPAS-1's launch slipped from a planned February liftoff to October for lack of a ride, Bakhai said.

SpaceX is reportedly not accepting new bookings until at least 2029. In addition, Skyroot Aerospace, which in July became the first Indian company to reach orbit, is still flying development missions meant to validate its Vikram-1 rocket before it begins full-scale commercial operations.

"There is a challenge right now in terms of availability of launch vehicles," Bakhai said. Once additional Indian rockets, such as those built by Skyroot and Agnikul, are flying regularly, "things will be much easier."

SatLeo is among more than 400 space startups that have emerged in India since the government opened the sector to private participation in 2020. Driven by this new wave of private enterprise, the country's space economy — currently valued at about $9 billion — is estimated to reach $40 billion over the next decade.

Asked what advice they would give newcomers entering the growing industry, SatLeo's three co-founders offered a unified message for success: start with the problem, then decide what to build.

"If you're solving a problem," Bhati said, "then people will bet on you."

Sharmila Kuthunur is an independent space journalist based in Bengaluru, India. Her work has also appeared in Scientific American, Science, Astronomy and Live Science, among other publications. She holds a master's degree in journalism from Northeastern University in Boston.

#791. Germany news: Parliament agrees on debt-laden 2027 budget

The budget committee in the Bundestag worked into the night to sign off on next year's spending plans. These include levels of new debt only eclipsed once, at the height of the COVID pandemic.

These updates have been closed. Below, you can review our collection of news and analysis on stories from or relating to Germany from Friday, November 13.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz got a birthday cake at the UN climate summit in Turkey this week. But he wasn't there to eat it. Meanwhile, in Berlin, climate activists marked his 71st birthday on Friday with a symbolic chocolate cake. Their message: they too want to reach that age on a livable planet.

Fridays for Future is taking its demands to German streets. Demonstrations were planned in more than 70 German cities on Friday, November 13.

Under the slogan "Pay your climate debt," protesters in the German capital demanded more funding for climate protection and adaptation in developing countries, alongside a global phase-out of coal, oil and gas.

Germany provided €4.7 billion ($5.2 billion) in federal budget funds for international climate financing in 2025 — below its €6 billion pledge.

But the protest movement is no longer drawing the crowds it once did. In September 2019, Fridays for Future mobilized an estimated 1.4 million people across Germany. Five years later, that figure fell to around 75,000 at a comparable nationwide strike.

This comes as broader youth frustration with German politics grows. "I don't feel addressed by the chancellor unfortunately," Kim, a protester in Berlin, told DW.

From military service to affordable housing and climate policy, younger Germans are questioning whether their concerns are being heard.

A recent nationwide poll found that 82% of Germans believe politicians do not adequately represent young people's interests. Among 18- to 34-year-olds, just 5% trust Merz's conservatives to champion their concerns, compared with 3% for their Social Democratic coalition partners.

Merz is not the first German chancellor to miss a UN climate summit. And smaller demonstrations do not necessarily mean young Germans care less about climate change. But the contrast is striking: while the climate movement struggles to mobilize, dissatisfaction among younger voters extends well beyond environmental policy.

Julian Reichelt, formerly the editor-in-chief of Germany's top-selling tabloid Bild, says he was the target of an arson attack after his car was set on fire and largely destroyed in Berlin.

Now editor-in-chief of the right-wing online portal Nius that he co-founded, Reichelt said the arson attack took place in the Charlottenburg district of the German capital overnight.

Police confirmed the car was intentionally set alight, saying a passerby reported it shortly after 2 a.m. that morning. However, they did not name a suspect or potential personal motive at first, saying only that the fire department responded and extinguished the fire.

"It is completely clear that this was a targeted attack," Reichelt said, calling it an "attempt at intimidation against new free media that stand up against this left-wing extremism."

Similar arson attacks several years ago targeted cars belonging to a columnist for another Berlin newspaper, B.Z., with a left-wing group claiming responsibility in one case.

That said, Berlin also has a more general and fairly well documented problem with arson and vandalism targeting cars, with an average of roughly two a night being set alight in the capital city over recent years. Vandalism and insurance fraud are the most common reasons more generally.

Reichelt was fired from his prominent job at Bild in 2021 amid allegations of sexual harassment, accusations he always denied and referred to as a "smear campaign."

Lawmakers in the Bundestag have approved reforms that will provide additional powers to Germany's domestic and external intelligence agencies.

The changes will strengthen both the external Federal Intelligence Service (BND) and domestic intelligence service the BfV, formally titled the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution.

The law passed fairly comfortably in the federal Bundestag lower house of parliament, with 309 votes in favor, 190 against and 71 abstentions.

The BfV will be granted powers beyond intelligence gathering and monitoring individuals, such as being able to secretly enter homes or take action against explosives or weapons.

In the case of the BND, it will be granted additional operational intervention powers, for instance moving to disable servers belonging to state-sponsored hacker groups abroad.

The changes aim to respond to intensified and evolving threats from foreign intelligence services and their partners, and to reduce dependency on information supplied by friendly foreign intelligence services.

Opposition parties have accused the government of abolishing or weakening the separation between the police and intelligence services — a sensitive and closely monitored distinction in German society, because of the legacy both of Adolf Hitler's Nazi regime and of the secret police services in Communist East Germany during the Cold War.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Friedrich Merz has said during his visit to Dublin that Germany and Europe's position in future peace talks for Ukraine is "set."

Following the talks in Abu Dhabi this week between Ukraine and Russia brokered by the US, which also involved European representatives at times, Merz said further negotiations were now planned.

"In the coming weeks there should now be concrete peace talks in which Europe is represented," Merz told reporters in Dublin amid an informal meeting of EU leaders.

He said that "provisionally" this might involve the same "group of Europeans" who had participated in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday.

"Germany is set in there, that is completely clear," he said.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz's call to link EU budget negotiations to the provision of assistance to Ukraine, which faced hefty criticism at home, has found some backing amid European Political Community meetings and an AI summit in Dublin.

Merz, who has been leading the charge to find savings in the next EU budget, said doing so could ensure stronger contributions to helping Ukraine from all EU member states.

Estonia's Prime Minister Kristen Michal said during the meeting in Dublin that he approved of Merz's suggestion "that support for Ukraine is also a part of our core security and our core financing."

He said that members who wanted a new EU budget should contribute.

Latvia's Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, meanwhile, said he agreed completely with Merz.

"We must all pull in the same direction. All of Europe must do its part," he said.

Luxembourg's Luc Frieden also said that "we must all stand behind Ukraine" and added that collective financial commitments should be a part of this.

As the largest economy and most populous country in the EU, Germany is the largest overall contributor both to the EU budget and to assistance for Ukraine.

Countries that tend to be so-called net beneficiaries of the EU budget, rather than net contributors to it, tend to be more reticent to cut spending plans.

Hosts Ireland, in a tricky position as the holders of the rotating presidency of the EU trying to broker a deal on the next seven-year budget, said it had concerns about adding an additional factor to the stalled talks, as the current budget's expiry at the end of 2027 starts to draw near.

"But I do understand why this is happening," Taoiseach (or prime minister) Micheal Martin said in Dublin. "Some countries have made considerable contributions and they want all EU member states to contribute financially to the support for Ukraine."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) was critical of both the spending and the fundraising plans in the 2027 budget, claiming without showing its workings that it would be able to do more with less by making swingeing cuts in various key areas.

Budget policy spokesman Michael Espendiller said the budget meant "more debts and more taxes and more burdens for the taxpayer."

He accused the Christian Democrats of breaking key election pledges by raising taxes on alcohol and tobacco. He then complained that despite this, there was not enough money for the promised electricity tax cut.

"If you put it into figures, the federal government will be taking out almost €400,000 (around $440,000) every minute in new debt," Espendiller said, calling for an end to what he called a spiral of debt.

He claimed that the AfD would have able to complete its budget with new debt of just €63 billion, not roughly €210 billion, while simultaneously providing tax relief of around €44 billion.

Espendiller said this would be achieved with wide-reaching cuts in several core areas of spending: climate protection, contributing to the EU budget and other EU funding, asylum-related spending, international development aid, and weapons deliveries and other assistance to Ukraine.

It's unclear to what extent these proposed cuts would be feasible or legal, or what domestic or international implications they might have, or whether they'd save anything like the amount the AfD asserts in practice.

Politicians on the Bundestag budget committee burned the proverbial candle at both ends heading into Friday morning, trying to finalize details of the federal government's spending plans for 2027 before the year's end.

The session took over 15 hours, and already politicians are talking about areas where they still see room for further improvement or alteration — but the document does at least stand in such a form in which it can take effect without too many complications.

Including all spending plans, in the core budget and from the so-called "special funds" for infrastructure and military modernization, new debt constitutes around a third of oultays.

In total, the plan is to take out new debt worth just over €210 billion ($233 billion), while taking in a little less than €400 billion in taxes.

That's the second-highest level of new debt in the post-war history of the Federal Republic of Germany. Even at the height of the COVID pandemic in 2021, new debt was only slightly higher, at €215.4 billion.

We'll likely be returning to the various details of and reactions to this story throughout the morning.

The environmentalist Greens took aim at Chancellor Merz for not delivering on a promise to reduce taxes on electricity in the final budget.

"The big promise that Chancellor Merz made a few days ago, sinking electricity taxes for everyone, this promise remains a broken promise," party co-leader Britta Hasselmann said on ZDF television on Friday.

"It was possible to find a way at short notice for several other things in this budget," she said.

"I think this demonstrates the inadequate planning and the weak leadership of the chancellor," Hasselmann said.

She added that the CDU forcing a delay to the planned sugar tax at short notice was further evidence of the planning shortcomings.

A budget expert at the party, Sebastian Schäfer, similarly alleged a "leadership vacuum in this coalition government," saying that what was put forward was less a budget and more a "wooden shack wihtout foundations."

The Left Party's budget policy spokesman Dietmar Bartsch has lamented a "knot garden of debt, tricks and delays," accusing the coalition of not conducting "responsible budgetary policy."

Despite criticizing the debt levels, Bartsch also said it was "deeply unserious" to float electricity tax relief but then withdraw the plan.

He said this would have cost less money than the federal government's plan to buy a share of the arms company KNDS. He also said it was unacceptable for the center-left Social Democrats to be celebrating just because "the odd welfare cut is not happening."

Ines Schwerdtner, co-leader of the party that firmly opposes defense spending and is at best lukewarm on NATO membership, said the record spending showed that money was not as tight as Merz's government made out.

"The debt brake is suspended for weapons, but for housing and electricity taxes they scrimp for every euro," Schwerdtner said. "The money is there, this government is just distributing it completely incorrectly."

Schwerdtner, herself a member of the budget committed in the Bundestag, called it a "budget of naivete."

More on this morning's top story in Berlin, the 2027 budget being signed off.

As the CDU calls for further savings, the Social Democrats say that the energy tax relief recently touted by Chancellor Friedrich Merz "would have to be financed with additional debts."

Ahead of Thursday's marathon talks, Merz had said he hoped to introduce the tax relief amid the stress caused by issues including the wars in Iran and Ukraine.

The SPD's Dirk Wiese said the junior coalition partners were "not disinclined to pave the way for the electricity tax relief," but not by making cuts elsewhere.

Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil of the SPD had said he did not see enough fiscal wiggle room to enable the desired tax break.

Bremen's mayor Andreas Bovenshulte, also a Social Democrat, said that while he would have welcomed the relief, other decisions meant it wasn't possible.

"For that, a serious financing source would have been required, for instance with a plastic or sugar of windfall tax," Bovenschulte said, in reference to either delayed or proposed but rejected plans to potentially increase tax revenues.

German defense industry startup Quantum Systems said its drones were operational worldwide once again, including with the Bundeswehr military, after a cyberattack by "hostile actors" last month.

The company had announced the cyberattack on Thursday, amid reporting from the Financial Times that also said the Bundeswehr had grounded its drones from the company.

"The fleet is operating normally around the globe — including Germany and the Bundeswehr," a Quantum Systems spokesperson said in an emailed statement to the Reuters news agency. "The Bundeswehr was the only customer to ground their systems as a precaution."

The company, based near Munich, had earlier said it uncovered an "active cyberattack" by hostile actors.

"The threat was contained thanks to the swift response of our IT and security teams in close and transparent collaboration with the authorities," it said in a statement, adding there was no risk for end users and operators using its unmanned systems.

Quantum drones are used by Ukrainian armed forces in their defensive war against Russia, among others.

"Companies at the forefront of supporting Ukraine are being targeted precisely because our work is critically relevant to customers' security," the company said. "Being aware of this responsibility, Quantum Systems has mitigation plans in place and strives to fulfil the highest standard of data and system security."

Senior Christian Democrat Union (CDU) politician Matthias Middelberg appeared on ZDF television this morning to discuss the budget breakthrough.

He identified one "weak point" after the overnight negotiations.

"We have not yet saved enough, we still need to save a lot more," he said.

Middelberg said that in his view the government would not be able to "collect the funds," because that would put too much tax strain on people and businesses.

Therefore, he said, "the government must make cutbacks."

Middelberg acepted that it wasn't clear how to do this, speculating that "perhaps there are subsidies or some other things" that could be ripe to be trimmed.

He said the leadership of the coalition government's CDU/CSU and Social Democrats would "consider this question very closely once more."

The German government statistics agency Destatis has published new figures on insolvency filings for the month of August.

A total of 2,067 companies registered insolvencies with German courts during the month, Destatis said, 4.4% more than in the same month in 2025.

The data operates on something of a delay, because the government tracks when courts grant the status, which can be almost three months after the initial application at times.

The increase has been a rolling trend this year. From January to August, 17,252 companies have filed for insolvency, 6.6% more than in the same period last year.

However, the total sum of debts forgiven in insolvency proceedings is actually quite considerably lower than in the first eight months of last year, at €25.9 billion ($28.7 billion) rather than €37.2 billion, because fewer large companies have gone bust.

More individuals are also filing for bankruptcy protection than in 2025, although the rise is somewhat less sharp. In August, 6,301 people gained insolvency protection, 2.8% more than last August. For January through August, the year-on-year increase is more modest, at 1.2%.

Politicians on the Bundestag budget committee burned the proverbial candle at both ends heading into Friday morning, trying to finalize details of the federal government's spending plans for 2027 before the year's end.

Moin! Here's hoping you slept more and better than the Bundestag's budget committee. Or if not, at least let's hope that you had more fun.

Its members worked towards the dawn in a session lasting over 15 hours, trying to iron out the last wrinkles in spending plans for 2027.

The proverbial white smoke emerged at around 6 in the morning in Berlin, with word of a finalized agreement.

If you were tired of talk and criticism of the "debt brake" and the "black zero" (a promise not to take any new debts) in the years following the eurozone debt crisis, rest assured we can assign such chatter to the history books for now.

The borrowing plans for 2027 — if you incorporate new debt taken out as part of so-called "special funds," for instance for the military and infrastructure, rather than as part of the core budget — are the second highest in the history of post-war Germany.

The country only took out more new debt in 2021, at the height of the COVID pandemic and even then it was very close indeed.

We'll bring you more news and reactions on this, and whatever else breaks around the country, as Friday develops.

#790. Mathematicians astounded by AI and human-written proofs of iconic Riemann hypothesis

In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

The Riemann hypothesis has been a lodestar for generations of mathetmaticians. Credit: James Brittain/Getty

In a year that has seen artificial intelligence reach one spectacular mathematical breakthrough after another, Anthropic has now claimed the top prize of them all: a full proof of the Riemann hypothesis, the statement that many mathematicians consider the most important open problem in the field. But on the same day as the Anthropic claim, a separate study claiming to have proven the Riemann also emerged — and this one is entirely human written.

The Anthropic announcement came on 20 November from Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at the San Francisco, California company. “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,” Alpöge wrote, referring to Anthropic’s large language model (LLM).

“If this fully checks out, it is clearly a historic milestone in mathematics,” says number theorist James Maynard, a Fields Medal winner at the University of Oxford, UK, says.

Anthropic AI ‘formalizes’ proof of Fermat’s last theorem — a milestone for mathematics

Anthropic AI ‘formalizes’ proof of Fermat’s last theorem — a milestone for mathematics

Hours later, Ravi Vakil, a mathematician at Stanford University in California, posted online a rival preprint to Alpöge’s, in what Vakil called a “hurried announcement.” The preprint was written by Alessandro Maria Masullo, a mathematician who received his PhD at Stanford in 2020 under the supervision of number theorist Brian Conrad. “The hope was to have Brian work with Alessandro for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people,” Vakil wrote. “Now it seems best to put out the current draft.”

The confirmation of either or both solutions would be a spectacular bicentenary present for Bernhard Riemann, the German mathematician who was born 200 years ago this September and who formulated the problem, which addresses the distribution of prime numbers, in the mid-1800.

The Riemann hypothesis is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems selected by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which has its scientific headquarters in Oxford, UK , at the turn of the twenty-first century. The institute offers a US$1 million prize to anyone who devises a solution to one of the problems, which are considered some of the most challenging in the field. Mathematicians using AI tools announced earlier this year that they had solved another Millennium problem, related to the Navier-Stokes equation.

The problem has to do with the ‘Riemann ζ function’ (ζ is the Greek letter zeta), which encodes the randomness properties of the prime numbers. Riemann discovered that the distribution of primes is encoded in the ζ function’s ‘zeroes.’ These are points, denoted by z, on a plane satisfying the equation ζ(z) = 0.

Riemann conjectured that apart from some obvious but uninteresting cases, all such solutions had to lie on a certain vertical line in the plane. If this were true, he showed, it would imply that prime numbers are scattered among all whole numbers in a way that is essentially as random as it could be.

Alpöge’s 4-page document includes a sketch of the proof. But Andrew Granville, a number theorist at the University of Montreal in Canada, says that Alpöge should have taken the time to prepare a clearer write-up before making the announcement, which came just days after Anthropic’s initial public offering (IPO). The IPO initially valued the company at US$1.5 trillion, but the company’s valuation dropped on 19 November.

“What he released is garbled,” Granville says of Alpöge’s document. Granville cites the downturn in the company’s stock value as the reason for the timing of the proof’s release.

“There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false,” Alpöge wrote in the document.

Anthropic did not respond immediately to Nature’s request for comment.

Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematician at New York University who collaborated with Alpöge on a separate project regarding the Navier-Stokes equation, says that Alpöge deserves a lot of credit for developing techniques to produce mathematical results using LLMs. “Levent himself built this amazing setup to do math”. He adds that Alpöge, who is himself a number theorist on leave from Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts, has been working relentlessly for months on this and other problems, hardly ever getting any sleep.

‘The job description is changing’: mathematician Terence Tao on the rise of AI

‘The job description is changing’: mathematician Terence Tao on the rise of AI

“I suspect that the proof will turn out to be correct,” Maynard says of the Alpöge announcement, even though it is now in the form of incomprehensible code in the Lean programming language.

“At the moment, it apparently is crazily complicated. It’s going to take a long time for mathematicians to digest,” says Buckmaster. Maynard agrees, but he adds, “assuming we do get the corresponding understanding, this will surely be viewed as one of the absolute pinnacles of mathematical results”.

The Lego Star Trek: U.S.S. Enterprise Bridge diorama is a wonderful bit of nostalgia and a stunning recreation of a sci-fi icon. The playset features arguably feel a little out of place, given that the audience for this set will be older fans who want to board the Starship Nostalgia. But maybe that's the whole point: Making old Trek more accessible to young 'uns.

Beautiful diorama recreating the iconic sci-fi set.

Why you can trust Space.com Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test and review products.

It's not quite a five-year mission, but as Star Trek celebrated its 60th anniversary in September of this year (we may have mentioned it once or twice), I decided it was high time I finally watched the original Star Trek.

Before this year, I hadn't seen a single episode of "Star Trek: The Original Series", as it's now known. I'm a millennial; I grew up on "The Next Generation", "Deep Space Nine" and "Voyager". By comparison, the old series (TOS) always looked so… old and naff whenever I saw clips of it.

But now I have seen the original series. Over the course of 2026, I've ploughed through all 79 episodes, spread across three seasons. And you know what? It's pretty damn good. Even with the shiny 2006 remasters, you'll have to prepare yourself for some bad special effects work, but the scripts are interesting, the sci-fi concepts are out there, and the acting — especially from Shatner and Nimoy — is top-notch.

And just as I finally discovered a love for this classic sci-fi series, what should drop into my lap? Why it's the new Star Trek: U.S.S. Enterprise NCC-1701 Bridge diorama set from Lego. Now I have more on my wishlist to add to the Best lego space sets.

Let's start with the Band-Aid rip: this set is $200. I know; it stings, especially when Star Trek promised us a future where money doesn't exist. But at 1701 pieces (nice, I see what you did there), it's much better value from a bricks-per-dollar perspective than the X-Files set we checked out recently.

Still, that's no small investment for a toy, even if it will make a lovely display piece when it's built.

As the name suggests, you get a full Lego-ified recreation of the bridge of the USS Enterprise (NCC-1701, no A, B, C, or D). This includes Captain Kirk's chair, the helm positions ahead of him (manned by Chekov and Sulu), and all of the surrounding computer displays where you usually find Spock, Uhura and Scotty.

There's even a viewscreen that can sit in front of the crew, displaying an adorable Klingon commander facing off against Kirk.

Board the legendary starship and meet the crew of the U.S.S. Enterprise NCC-1701 for an amazing building experience. Recreate the iconic bridge and transporter room that served as the backdrop for epic scenes from "Star Trek: The Original Series".

Alongside the main bridge, there are a few fun extras bolted on, including a rotating transporter pad (which can make minifigures "disappear") and a working turbolift door connected to the back of the main bridge diorama. You'll have to make the swoosh sound effect yourself, though.

It's a wonderfully faithful recreation of Kirk's command center, complete with computer panels and screens, swiveling chairs and that weird scope thing that Spock was always looking into.

That said, it's a little lacking in proper Easter eggs. There are some tribbles hiding around the build, and the monitors have custom stickers showing cool Trekkie things. The weapon display racks on the back hold an array of pointy Klingon blades, Starfleet phasers, Sulu's fencing rapier and even Spock's harp, but compared to, say, the X-Files set we built recently, it feels a bit lacking in those deep-cut references.

All in all, it's a fantastic little diorama, but when it was announced, I'll admit I was a little puzzled as to who it was aimed at. "Star Trek fans, duh!" is the obvious response, but the Venn diagram crossover between "people who are nostalgic for the original series of Star Trek" and "people who want to buy $200 Lego sets" has to be pretty small, right?

Star Trek first aired way back in 1966, which means the first generation of fans are now 70 years old and upwards. Lord knows I hope I'm still building Lego sets when I'm 70, but is that a large enough crowd to make this set a success? Then again the show was repeated and syndicated throughout the 70s and 80s, which means hopefully there'll be some younger buyers, too.

The playset aspects of the set are even more puzzling. The working door, exploding monitor and spinning transporter pad are great additions to a kids' playset, but this isn't that — it's a display for nostalgic Star Trek fans. The design of the set just feels a bit confused.

But then it hit me. Maybe this isn't just for fans of the original series; maybe it's meant to create some new fans. I started watching the original Star Trek 60 years after its debut because… well, I'm the sci-fi editor for a space website, and it felt wrong that I hadn't seen it. But most people don't have that sort of professional impetus. The average person won't jump back to watch a 60-year-old TV show without a polite nudge, and this set does a great job of highlighting the charm and optimism of Star Trek's debut outing.

I don't know, maybe I'm just projecting here. Maybe Lego bought the rights to make Star Trek sets and needed something to do after they'd mined all the nostalgia they could from the excellent Enterprise D set they released in 2025. Maybe this is just a toy for big kids.

Or maybe… just maybe, it's meant to inspire the next generation of Star Trek fans to check out where the magic started.

Disclaimer: We were sent a copy of the Star Trek: U.S.S. Enterprise NCC-1701 Bridge set by Lego.

Ian is the Entertainment Editor at Space.com, covering movies, TV series, and games in the space and sci-fi realms. He's a massive sci-fi nerd and has been writing about games and entertainment for over eight years, with articles on sites like Space, LiveScience, GamesRadar, and more. With a degree in biology, a PhD in chemistry, and his previous role at the Institute of Physics Publishing, Ian is taking a world tour through the different scientific disciplines.

Stassi Schroeder shared her reaction to ex Jax Taylor’s cancer diagnosis in an exclusive interview with E! News during People and InStyle’s Drive-By Party in Las Vegas.

Stassi Schroeder makes it a rule not to comment on her ex Jax Taylor.

“One of confusion,” Schroeder exclusively told E! News at People and InStyle’s Drive-By Party at the Las Vegas Grand Prix Nov. 20. “I'm not here to doubt somebody's diagnosis. I hope the best for everyone involved.”

As for whether she has a message for Taylor, she simply noted, “no.”

But Schroeder—whose relationship with Taylor was chronicled during their time on Vanderpump Rules—isn’t on the outs with all of her former costars. After all, Katie Maloney accompanied the You Can’t Have It All author to the event.

“Well, Katie Maloney is here with me right now,” Schroeder noted, “so her.”

And while the 38-year-old—who shares kids Hartford, 5, and Messer, 3, with husband Beau Clark—may be tight-lipped about where she stands with her fellow reality stars, she’s also not interested in clearing up any rumors floating around about them.

“You know what, let's just let them all live,” she said. “Let's let them all go and let everyone run with them.”

Taylor, 47, shared he was diagnosed with cancer after a tumor was discovered on his kidney during treatment for kidney stones in July.

“This is something I’ve kept private for the past few months because it’s been one of the scariest times of my life,” he wrote in a Nov. 19 Instagram post, which featured photos from his hospital bed and a video of him walking with the help of a walker. “What I thought was just a kidney stone turned into something I never imagined. My CT scan also showed a tumor on my left kidney. After many tests and appointments I found out it was cancer.”

Taylor—who shares 5-year-old son Cruz with estranged wife Brittany Cartwright—shared that the diagnosis was especially challenging given his father had died of cancer. As he said of the moment he learned of his diagnosis, “It broke me.”

As a part of his treatment, the reality TV star underwent surgery in which a source close to Taylor exclusively told E! News Nov. 19 that he’d experienced "some complications.”

However, the source noted that through it all, Taylor has had his girlfriend Lori Krebs by his side.

"The last few months have really taken a toll on him and she’s always been someone who brings him a sense of peace,” the source said. “They’ve been through a lot together and there’s a very deep love and connection between them."

The insider added, "They’re truly there for one another, and I think going through something like this has only made them realize just how much they mean to each other."

#786. Brooks Nader Reveals If She Approves of Sister Dating Pete Davidson

Brooks Nader addressed speculation that her sister Sarah Jane Nader is dating Pete Davidson during an exclusive interview with E! News at People and InStyle’s Drive-By Party in Las Vegas Nov. 20.

Brooks Nader loves thy sister Sarah Jane Nader, but she isn’t too thrilled about a potential update on her love life.

Amid rumors her younger sister is dating Pete Davidson, the Baywatch actress shared her thoughts on the speculation.

“I don’t approve of it. No,” Brooks exclusively told E! News at People and InStyle’s Drive-By Party at the Las Vegas Grand Prix Nov. 20 as she gave a thumbs-down to the camera. “She can do whatever she wants, but I’m not into it.”

And according to the 29-year-old, she’s not always privy to details about Sarah Jane’s dating life.

“You’d have to ask her,” Brooks said of how long her sister and Pete have been seeing each other. “She doesn’t get into it with me. When she knows I don’t approve of someone, she doesn’t tell me anything, so I find out online.”

While the Sports Illustrated model made her views on Sarah Jane potentially dating the comedian clear, a source close to Pete previously told E! News there is no truth to the dating rumors.

In fact, while it’s been nearly four months since the Dancing With the Stars alum and Bodies Bodies Bodies actor made waves when they stepped out together in Brooklyn, the source noted that they’ve only seen each other a handful of times since.

For the August outing, Sarah Jane, 24, and Pete, 33, were spotted getting into a car together. The Meet Cute actor opened the passenger door for the Love They Nader star, before he moved over to the driver’s side. But at the time, a source with direct knowledge told E! News the duo are just friends.

As for Brooks, the news of her sister hanging out with Pete—dad to daughter Scottie, 11 months, with ex Elsie Hewitt—was unexpected.

“Oh wow, I thought she was into girls this week,” she joked to TMZ after Sarah Jane and Pete’s night out. “That’s what her vibe has been.”

The model added that she needed to chat with Sarah Jane, jokingly admitting that she was “confused” and “lost” about the rumors.

“I really did think that she was into girls recently,” Brooks quipped, “but she keeps us on our toes.”

While it’s unclear what the future will hold for Sarah Jane’s love life, keep reading for a closer look at Brooks’ dating history…

Leaving her Louisiana home to pursue her modeling dreams at the age of 19, Brooks Nader knew she had to make some big deals. "When I moved to New York, my dad was like, 'You're living a full-ride scholarship. I have no money to support your life in New York. You better find a boyfriend,'" she explained to People. "Which I did, thank God, for just the rent purposes."

Though, she arguably grew quite fond of advertising executive Billy Haire, the duo marrying in New Orleans' French Quarter in December 2019.

Her mom and dad were less than thrilled to hear about their separation nearly five years later. "When I told my parents I was getting divorced, you’d think I killed somebody," she shared on the Love Thy Nader reality series she filmed with sisters Sarah Jane Nader, Grace Ann Nader and Mary Holland Nader. "They were like, 'This is the worst decision ever. Divorce is a sin.'"

But the Sports Illustrated Swimsuit model would beg to differ. "Once I got to that other side, I realized, 'Wait, I got me. I can do anything I f--king put my mind to,'" she reflected to Bustle in 2025. "I was with someone for 10 years, and I cut it off and came out better. I can push out a human; I can start a company; I can get over anybody. It’s euphoric, that feeling."

As for Billy, he went on to charm another reality star, he and Southern Charm alum Naomie Olindo announcing their engagement in December 2025.

In the months following Brooks' divorce, it seemed she had snagged a pass from retired NFL quarterback Tom Brady. Though she and the NFL on Fox color commentator were spotted at Michael Rubin’s 2024 Fourth of July party in the Hamptons, any fireworks had dissipated by fall.

"She’s having fun as a single girl," sister Sarah Jane told Daily Mail that September. "I think it’s as exciting as it possibly could be."

Cast on Dancing With the Stars shortly after her 2024 divorce, Brooks was eyeing more than just the mirrorball trophy. Paired with pro Gleb Savchenko, the two quickly became partners IRL as well.

But much like their dances, their romance was largely physical. Single for the first time since she was 18, and doing the tango with "the hottest guy I've ever seen in my life," she detailed on Love Thy Nader, meant things escalated quickly.

"All we did was have sex," Brooks shared on the Freeform series, "because I didn't really talk to him that much."

Perhaps that lack of communication is why he felt blindsided when she confirmed in April 2025 that they were no longer in step.

They weren't even following the same routine, to be honest. "I was surprised to learn through an article published today … that Brooks has ended our relationship," Gleb said in an April 7 statement to Us Weekly. "The last communication I received from her was a text on April 6, asking to speak. I called her today in response, but she has not replied."

Jimmy Kimmel took a swing at getting Nader to confirm the rumors she was matched up with tennis phenom Jannik Sinner. "Are you dating Italian superstar Jannik Sinner?" he asked during her September 2025 appearance on Jimmy Kimmel Live. Her response? "Is this like an interrogation? I'm so scared right now."

Though she suggested Stephen Colbert could potentially serve up the truth. "Well, ask Stephen what match we were at," she said of sitting next to the late-night host during her Aug. 31 outing to the U.S. Open. Because, as she noted of Sinner, "I don't think he was at that one. You're close. You're warm, but we weren't at that match."

What Brooks was trying to hint at in her back-and-forth volley on Kimmel was that she'd found a potential partner in Spanish athlete Carlos Alcaraz. "The rumors are true," sister Grace Ann exclusively told E! News at the Raising Cane's New York Fashion Week Show days later. Still, she cautioned it wasn't exactly love-all just yet. "Dating is such a loose term," she added. "But I do know he’s the man of the hour."

And while she was waiting for an introduction, he'd already made the acquaintance of their other sisters. "I'm dying to," Grace Ann said of meeting the seven-time Grand Slam champ. "Such a cutie."

As for those finding fault with the swimsuit model doubling up with the tennis stars, "I mean, dating is such a loose term these days," she mused during a September 2025 appearance on Watch What Happens Live. "Guys do it all the time. So why can’t I do it?"

Oh, how it felt so real when Rocketman actor Taron Egerton held his tiny dancer close during a March 28, 2026 date night in Los Angeles. Following a three-hour dinner at Capo in Santa Monica, Calif., he and Brooks walked arm-in-arm to nearby Shutters on the Beach to drink each other in.

#785. 'Rolls-Royce' Iqbal's 'dream' journey from Old Trafford to Tannadice

Jim Goodwin's side are eight games unbeaten, with Zidane Iqbal pivotal

Given the superlatives being thrown in the direction of Zidane Iqbal by the Scottish football fraternity, one would think he was a replica of a certain France great instead of just sharing his name.

So much so that BBC Radio Scotland pundits were suggesting on Saturday's Sportsound that the 23-year-old is the answer to Celtic's hunt for a long-term successor to captain Callum McGregor as their midfield general.

It is just as well for Dundee United that the Iraq international is tied to them until at least the summer, his early season appearances for Utrecht ruling out a transfer during the January window.

So, where has he sprung from and what is all the fuss about?

Hibs 0-4 Dundee United: What Goodwin said

Born in Manchester to a Pakistani father and an Iraqi mother, Iqbal came through the Old Trafford youth system.

He signed his first professional contract with United in 2021 and became the first British-born South Asian and first-ever British South Asian to play in the Champions League when he came on as an 89th-minute substitute against Young Boys that December.

However, that was to be his one and only first-team appearance and, although he had already made his international debut in a World Cup qualifier at the age of 19, he was sold to Utrecht for a reported fee of Â£1m in summer 2023.

Starting off in their Jong Utrecht second string, he would go on to make 49 appearances for the Dutch top-flight outfit before making a surprise switch to the Scottish Premiership this summer.

On the one hand, United were getting a player who played all three of Iraq's games at this summer's World Cup, two of them starts, albeit all three were heavy defeats.

On the other hand, Iqbal had only managed seven appearances last season for Utrecht and had been a second-half substitute in two of their four matches at the start of the new campaign.

However, after a pivotal display in what was being described as a midfield "masterclass" by United in Saturday's 4-0 dismantling of hosts Hibernian, manager Jim Goodwin revealed he always had belief the Tangerines were unearthing a "Rolls-Royce".

"The head of recruitment's job is to go and identify good talent for us," Goodwin told BBC Scotland. "It's my job to give him the profile and then he goes out and does the groundwork.

"We could see immediately when we watched the footage of Zidane and when we had the Zoom call with him and his representatives, we not only had a fantastic player but a really good person with the right characteristics to come and fit the culture here."

Zidane Iqbal was also a marked man at the World Cup finals

While on-loan Rangers man Lyall Cameron was among the goals and fellow 24-year-old Dylan Tait provided a stylish assist, it was the third leg of what some regard as the best midfield triumvirate in the Premiership who was singled out for most praise at Easter Road.

With former Celtic winger Aidan McGeady again pondering the question about McGregor's likely successor, transfer market expert and former United wing-back Allan Preston opined: "A six for Celtic? Look no further than young Iqbal.

"He's been magnificent since he's come to Scottish football, absolutely brilliant. Running the show again.

"If Celtic are looking for a young boy at his age with experience, he is a full international, knows the game, played in Scotland, you can see what he can do, there's your man in front of you.

"Other players' hair's on fire, but he's just nice and calm. He's at a different level. He doesn't panic. When the ball comes to him, he is so calm on it, he takes his time, he's got great peripheral vision."

The former Dundee United wing-back pointed out, though: "He's had his two clubs that he can play for in a year of football, so he is going nowhere until at least the summer, so enjoy him while you can because I think you'll get serious money for this young boy."

McGeady pointed to Iqbal's "good pedigree", having started with Manchester United and already having 32 caps for Iraq, but wondered if that would be enough for Celtic to consider him.

"I don't even think, if he's performing this well, Celtic will go and get him," said McGeady.

"Why are Celtic not looking at players like this? Do they feel they have to prove themselves somewhere else first?"

Former Celtic captain Scott Brown was similarly impressed.

"He's been a delight to watch - sharpness to get on the ball and willingness to drive forward," the former midfielder and manager pointed out.

"He beats a man in the middle of the park as well and there's not too many midfielders willing to do that.

"Watching him there talking to the media, he can't get the smile off his face. He enjoys football, he takes the ball under pressure, he does things that other people don't do, especially in midfield.

"He brings composure, but he can also drive through as well. His willingness to keep getting on the ball, even if he makes that slight mistake - that's what I really enjoy watching about him."

While Goodwin reckons there will be likely interest in the summer, Iqbal has no thoughts of so quickly leaving a club - and manager - who have resurrected his club career.

"I'm not even looking at any other clubs," he told BBC Scotland. "I'm fully focused on Dundee United.

"They've given me a platform to enjoy myself and play football. I'm really enjoying my football again.

"They've given me faith and confidence. The gaffer and the coaching staff have a lot of belief in me.

"The bare minimum I can do is pay them back with strong performances and hopefully it carries on."

Iqbal recalled being at Manchester United's "development centre since I was four or five - I signed when I was eight", explaining that he "then left for some first-team football".

He stressed that his lack of games last season came as a result of "a couple of injuries" and, while "I learnt a lot in Holland", he is "happy to have left that behind me", adding: "That book's closed now."

Visit our Dundee United page for all the latest news, analysis and fan views

Get Dundee United news notifications in the BBC Sport app

Iqbal also recalled how Goodwin's enthusiasm persuaded him to make the switch to Tannadice on deadline day.

"After the World Cup, I had one year left on my contract and I was in touch with my agent," the midfielder said. "We both wanted a move and I had a few chats with a few clubs.

"To be fair, I left it a bit late for Dundee United, but after the first call with the gaffer, I straight away called my agent after we ended the call.

"I said, 'look, I genuinely feel like the guy really believes in me'.

"It happened very late. I had to drive from Holland to Scotland. It was a tough drive but worth it in the end."

That World Cup was also a defining experience, with representing his country in the United States described as surreal.

"Having your friends and family there to watch you and playing on the world stage, with so many people, was a dream," he said.

"Playing against top players gave me that confidence boost I needed. I thought I did well in the three tough games.

"I knew, wherever I'd end up, with the faith of the gaffer, I could really kick on and push because I've learnt so much from the World Cup."

Goodwin is the manager to have done that and Iqbal added: "He's such a top guy, not just in football.

"His tactics are amazing. Everyone's comfortable. Everyone wants to fight for him."

#784. Miley Cyrus, Maxx Morando Host Rehearsal Dinner Ahead of Wedding

Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando appeared to host a rehearsal dinner for their loved ones ahead of their fast-approaching wedding.

The climb to Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando’s wedding has officially begun.

After all, the Hannah Montana alum’s stepsister Lily-Rose Purcell shared special details from what appeared to be the couple’s rehearsal dinner Nov. 20—and it’s hard not to adore the sweet glimpse.

Plus, it’s clear that Cyrus, 33, and Morando, 28, can expect to receive their flowers for the event’s gorgeous set-up as one snap shared to Purcell’s Instagram Stories captured a beautifully set circular table with the event’s dinner menu on full display.

Though the menu included a main course of filet mignon and Maine lobster ravioli, followed by a dessert selection of chocolate caramel layer cake, vanilla crème brûlée and raspberry sorbet, the sweetest element was the “M+M” printed at the top—a nod to the couple’s first initials.

Meanwhile, Purcell—whose father Dominic Purcell tied the knot with Cyrus’ mom Tish Cyrus in 2023—shared even more insight into the candlelit affair as she snapped a photo of her dessert plate, which featured three mini sweet treats.

But what’s a rehearsal dinner without a refreshment to take the edge off? In Purcell’s case, that would be an espresso martini, which was placed beside her plate alongside a glass of water while purple and pink flowers could be seen as centerpieces in the background.

The “Flowers” singer and Liily drummer confirmed their engagement in December 2025 after four years of dating.

And while nobody’s perfect in any relationship, Cyrus shared she had a very specific fear ahead of saying “I do” to the musician.

"We've been together six years, and I've never gotten the ick," she told Zane Lowe in an interview shared by Apple Music Sept. 17. "All of a sudden I got in my head, I was like, ‘Oh my God, we’re about to get married. What if I get the ick?'"

But Morando—who first met Cyrus on a blind date in 2021—had an answer that proved he could be the one.

"I asked him, 'What happens if you get the ick once you’re married?'" she continued. "He’s like, 'You deal with it and you move on and you don’t be a baby. The ick is for when you’re in fifth grade.'"

Even so, the Grammy winner is excited to bring her playful side into the couple’s next chapter.

As she put it, "I think that’s the thing that maybe generations prior didn’t teach us, that marriage doesn’t need to be a prison. It can actually be a playground."

Keep reading for more of Cyrus and Morando’s sweetest moments…

Miley Cyrus and musician Maxx Morando began dating in 2021. "We got put on a blind date," she recalled to British Vogue in 2023. "Well, it was blind for me and not really for him. I thought, 'The worst that can happen is I leave.'"

Miley didn't leave and, as their romance blossomed, the pair went red carpet official at the Gucci Love Parade event on November 2, 2021.

Miley and Maxx, who is a drummer in the band Liily, enjoyed a night out seeing Chicago on Broadway.

The "Flowers" singer and her boyfriend stepped out together at a Versace runway show in West Hollywood on March 9, 2023.

Maxx was by Miley's side when she won her first-ever Grammy at the 2024 award ceremony. The couple even shared a sweet smooch at their table during the event, and Miley referred to Maxx in her acceptance speech as "my love."

They returned to the Grammy Awards in 2025 for another public date night. "He’s very similar to me," Miley told Harper's Bazaar in an interview published November 2024. "We just don’t take life too seriously."

Maxx, who is six years younger than the Hannah Montana star, joined Miley on the red carpet at SNL50: The Anniversary Special, to celebrate 50 years of Saturday Night Live.

The musicians got glammed up for a big night out at the 2025 Oscars ceremony.

And later that night they stepped out in fresh looks for an appearance at the Vanity Fair Oscar Party.

It was a party in the U.S.A. when the pair got married in Plam Springs.

That's pretty close for such a colossal combustion.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A new supernova has been spotted exploding in the spiral galaxy NGC 1433, about 50 million light-years from Earth.

Researchers have discovered a new supernova called SN 2026ahvu. A Type Ia supernova, this event took place in a system with two stars orbiting one another (also known as a binary system), in which typically one star is an exploding white dwarf.

During most type Ia supernovae, the white dwarf pulls material away from the other star until enough accumulates on its surface to create an explosion.

Finding galaxies where stellar explosions are taking place isn't a rarity. However, this supernova is unique in how early it was captured. If the supernova were starting to dim, researchers might infer that the event was ending. However, according to details shared when it was first spotted, as well as later observations, this supernova was discovered while getting brighter.

This indicates that the supernova was likely caught early in the process of exploding, providing researchers with a unique opportunity to observe the event as it is taking place. By exploring observations of the galaxy before, during and (in the future) after the supernova event, researchers can investigate this type Ia supernova and how it affected the system in which it took place.

Scientists made this discovery using ATLAS, or the Asteroid Terrestrial-impact System, which is a robotic astronomical survey made up of telescopes across both hemispheres.

ATLAS is designed to spot incoming near-Earth objects like asteroids before they can reach Earth. It's essentially an asteroid impact early warning system.

But just because that's what the system is designed for doesn't mean that's all it can do. The system can also spot other objects moving through space and, in this instance, it was able to capture observations of this supernova.

Following its initial discovery, other observations of the supernova were made using NOIRLab's Dark Energy Camera (DECam) and Gemini South telescope.

Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. #782. Germany's Nmecha won't repeat controversial goal celebration

Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp has said midfielder Felix Nmecha will not repeat a goal celebration that sparked controversy over the past week. Germany are set to face Serbia and the Netherlands in the Nations League.

With the controversy sparked by Felix Nmecha's celebrations after his goals in Dortmund's 2-1 win over Elfersberg last weekend, the subject was always going to be top of reporters' minds when Germany coach Jürgen Klopp faced reporters ahead of Friday's match against Serbia.

Nmecha celebrated the goals by mimicking taking a crown off his head and kneeling to place it on the ground.

This was understood by many to be a nod to a Ballers in God (BIG) campaign called "The King's Return."

BIG, a Christian group for footballers, has said it aims to "demonstrate love and respect towards everyone," but critics claim it discriminates against the queer and transexual people. The discourse generated by the celebration did not go unnoticed by the Germany boss.

​Klopp told reporters in Belgrade on Thursday evening, that the 26-year-old Nmecha had assured him that he meant no harm by his actions.

"Last weekend I ​saw Felix score two great goals and saw the celebration and then the gesture. I thought nothing of it at the time, but then it all kicked off," he said.

"As the controversy escalated, I started looking into the details of the subject and trying to form a clear picture of it.

"I confronted him with all the things you (reporters) might have confronted him with. He told me that it had nothing to do with that at all, and that he loves all people and does not discriminate against anyone."

He then said that Nmecha had agreed not to repeat the celebration.

In Friday's match, Klopp's goal will be to keep alive Germany's chances of reaching the Nations League quarterfinals with a win over Serbia. Germany are third in Group A2 with 5 points, trailing the Netherlands and Greece, who both have 8. Serbia, who Germany beat 2-0 in Munich last month, are still without a win.

"We feel well prepared," Klopp said, adding that his team were committed to earning "a final" for the last group last group game on Monday in Berlin against the Netherlands.

Klopp also expressed his disappointment that only a few thousand Serbian children would be admitted to the stadium due to a spectator ban. Originally, the game was to be played behind closed doors after Serbia was sanctioned for racist and discriminatory behavior by its fans. However, a clause in the UEFA rules allows a selected group of guests to attend. Now children under 15 accompanied by teachers or football coaches are expected to be at the match.

"We're expecting some 5,000 guests," a spokesman for the Serbian FA told the DPA news agency. The stadium's capacity is 55,000. The German FA has been allocated just 50 tickets for its fans.

#781. Pepe did not injure eyes staring at sun, say Villarreal

Nicolas Pepe (right) wore an eye mask on his return to the side following his eye operation in October

Villarreal say reports striker Nicolas Pepe needed eye surgery because he stared directly at the solar eclipse are "completely false".

In a statement, the Spanish club said an operation in October that ruled the 31-year-old out for six matches was "scheduled in advance" and "entirely unrelated" to the eclipse, which took place on 12 August.

Reports on social media suggested the former Arsenal forward had injured his eyes staring directly at the sun during the lunar event, with a video then emerging - purportedly from one of Pepe's social media accounts - showing him watching it in Spain.

"Villarreal CF, in response to reports published in various media outlets recently, clarifies that it is completely false that Nicolas Pepe's eye surgery has any connection to viewing the solar eclipse," said the club.

"The surgery had been scheduled in advance for reasons entirely unrelated to this event.

"The club urges accuracy and responsibility when reporting on matters related to its players' health."

Staring at an eclipse without protection can damage the retina, which sits at the back of the eye, and particularly those cells responsible for sharp central vision.

In the build-up to this summer's event, experts warned only genuine specially-designed solar eclipse glasses should be used, and that ordinary sunglasses or other devices were not enough to prevent potential damage.

Pepe has scored 14 goals in 86 appearances in all competitions for Villarreal after joining from Trabzonspor in 2024.

He cost Arsenal a then-club record Â£72m when he joined from Lille in the summer of 2019.

Pepe scored 27 goals in 112 games for the Gunners and had a loan spell at Nice before joining Trabzonspor on a free transfer.

#780. Watford seek sixth manager in 18 months after sacking Dionisi

Alessio Dionisi was the fifth Italian manager hired by Watford under the ownership of the Pozzo family

Watford are looking for their sixth manager in 18 months after they sacked head coach Alessio Dionisi following 18 games in charge.

The 46-year-old Italian was appointed in June after the departure of Ed Still, who himself lasted only three months at Vicarage Road.

Still, Javi Gracia and Paulo Pezzolano were all also given full-time contracts after Tom Cleverley left in May 2025.

Dionisi was Watford's 12th head coach, not including interim bosses, since the end of the 2020-21 season, and leaves the Hornets searching for a 25th since the Pozzo family took over the club in 2012.

The club have had 57 permanent managers in their 145-year history.

The decision to replace him comes after Saturday's crushing 4-0 defeat by Sheffield United at Bramall Lane.

Dionisi's dismissal caps an underwhelming start to the season, with the Hornets having won just four league games to leave them 21st in the table.

"We thank Alessio and his staff for his professionalism and their efforts," sporting director Luke Dowling told the club website., external

"As I'm sure the supporters have seen, Alessio is a really good guy and we wish him the best for the future.

"The process has started for a replacement and we hope to be in a position to announce that shortly."

Dionisi was sacked by Serie B club Empoli in March after only five months in charge following a run of five wins in 22 matches.

His spell in charge of the Hornets was his first outside his homeland and started promisingly when his youthful side beat Southampton in their opening league game.

But they won only two of their next 12 in all competitions, and despite deservedly beating Charlton on 17 October, reverses at Wolves and Norwich followed, before four points from Dionisi's final three games in charge of the Hertfordshire side and his dismissal means further upheaval for the Hornets.

With more than a third of the league season complete, Watford are one place outside of the Championship relegation zone (table shown before Burnley face Blackburn on Sunday)

Since sacking Cleverley at the end of the 2024-25 campaign, the club has now been through four permanent head coaches, as well as interim boss Charlie Daniels' two-game spell in charge.

Of those four, only Gracia, in his second spell at Vicarage Road, took charge of more than 20 games.

On the morning of their final-day drubbing by Coventry last season, chief executive Scott Duxbury wrote a statement on the club website saying Watford had made mistakes, labelling their end to the campaign "unacceptable" and "truly disappointing in the extreme".

Fist my bump, everyone, because box office smash hit "Project Hail Mary" is heading back to theaters this December.

The exceptional sci-fi movie, based on Andy Weir's book, stars Ryan Gosling as Ryland Grace, a middle-school science teacher who becomes key to saving the world. Together with Rocky, an alien he meets along the way, Grace must solve the riddle of the mysterious substance that's causing the sun (and Rocky's star) to die out.

Amazon MGM has revealed the return to theaters with a video showcasing the many accolades that the film received. "Project Hail Mary" returns to the big screen on Dec. 11 and will be shown in all formats, including IMAX and 70MM.

"Project Hail Mary" was a massive success for Amazon MGM, grossing over $600 million worldwide when it first dropped in theaters back in March 2026. It was also a huge hit with critics, scoring an average of 95% on Rotten Tomatoes, and more importantly, getting two big thumbs up in our review!

Dec. 11 is a smart choice by MGM too, as it puts the sci-fi spectacle back in front of audiences a week ahead of Avengers: Doomsday and Dune: Part 3. That's not a battle you want to get in the middle of.

If you missed "Project Hail Mary" in theaters the first time, I'd definitely recommend you try to catch one of these screenings. It's a beautiful movie — visually and emotionally — and it deserves to be seen on the big screen.

If you're not feeling up to a trip to the theaters, you can also catch "Project Hail Mary" from the comfort of your own home, as it's also streaming on Amazon Prime Video.
